Event Description mention clearly and el:
Event Title: 60 Seconds: Chemical Apocalypse

Theme: Chemical Safety, Emergency Response, and Industrial Filtration

Event Overview
60 Seconds: Chemical Apocalypse is an intense, hands-on simulation where students step into the shoes of an emergency disaster response team. Following a sudden chemical leak at a plant, teams must think fast, manage limited resources, and solve real-world engineering problems under tight time pressure.

Starting with a fast-paced, 60-second material scramble, teams must build functional protection gear, stop chemical leaks, trade resources with rival teams, and spot fraudulent safety credentials—all using only the tools they manage to scavenge.

Core Engineering Concepts Covered
Chemical Adsorption & Filtration: Students learn why basic cloth fails against chemical vapors, seeing firsthand how activated charcoal actively traps toxic fumes at a microscopic level.
Airflow & Filter Design: Teams learn to balance filter density—making sure a mask is thick enough to catch toxins, but breathable enough for air to pass through.
Process Control & Isolation: Teams must identify and operate emergency shutdown valves to isolate leaking pipe sections, balancing system pressure changes to safely stop chemical releases at the source.
Industrial Safety Protocols: Solutions are judged on real industrial safety standards, teaching participants how real chemical engineers handle dangerous spills, toxic gases, and emergency gear ratings.
Rules of the Event, include how many rou:
Team Setup & Rules
Team Size: 2 to 5 participants per team.

The Designated Runner: Each team nominates one designated runner to enter the supply zone during the scramble.

Carrying Capacity Rule: The runner can carry a maximum of two items at a time (one in each hand). No bags, pockets, or extra containers may be used during the scramble.

Property Lock: Once the 60-second scramble ends, all collected items become the permanent property of that team for the remainder of the event, forming their sole survival inventory.

Phase-by-Phase Gameplay
Phase 1: The 60-Second Scramble
The Setup: A shared central table contains a limited pool of safety gear, laboratory tools, raw materials, and structural items.

The Action: At the sound of the emergency siren, the designated runner from each team enters the supply zone simultaneously.

The Scramble: The runner has 60 seconds to inspect the available inventory, select up to two items, run back to their team station to drop them off, and dash back to collect more. Teams must continuously communicate from their stations to tell their runner which specific items to prioritize before time expires.

Phase 2: Crisis Management & Problem Solving (Rounds 1–4)
Teams face sequential emergency scenario rounds representing escalating challenges within a breached chemical facility (e.g., acid spills, volatile gas leaks, structural breaches, or toxic runoff).

Teams must formulate and write down practical engineering solutions or fabricate physical functional setups using only the items in their inventory.

Phase 3: Internal Trading Window (Stage 5)
Duration: Exactly 60 seconds.

Mechanic: Teams enter an open negotiation market where they can barter and trade items directly with rival teams. A team lacking charcoal for gas filtration might trade excess duct tape or plastic equipment to another team in need of structural materials.

Phase 4: Advanced Scenarios & The External Visitor (Rounds 6–8+)
Crisis Progression: Scenarios become more complex, requiring multi-layered solutions (e.g., combined filtration, neutralization, and structural sealing).

The External Visitor Event (After Round 8): An unknown outside survivor/trader arrives at the facility offering a high-value trade proposition (e.g., trading rare filtration components for vital safety gear).

The Verification Challenge: Teams must analyze the visitor’s technical pitch, credentials, and offered materials to determine if they are genuine or a fraudulent imposter. Making a trade with a fake visitor results in losing valuable inventory for useless or compromised materials

Rube Wars is a team-based engineering challenge that tests creativity, mechanical thinking, teamwork, and problem-solving. Teams of 2–4 members will be given a specific target to accomplish along with a list of 15 available mechanisms.

The challenge is to design and build a working chain-reaction machine that achieves the given target using at least 6 and a maximum of 9 mechanisms from the provided list of 15  mechanisms. Teams will have limited time to plan, build, test, troubleshoot, and refine their machines.

The machine must successfully connect the selected mechanisms into a continuous sequence, where the completion of one mechanism triggers the next, ultimately achieving the given target.

Event Description mention clearly and el: Saponify and Aroma Lab are two hands-on, non-competitive chemistry workshops by ChES & IIChE Society, running side by side from 10 am to 5 pm in batches of 25 (about 150 participants each). No prior chemistry knowledge is needed, and every participant takes home what they make. In Saponify, participants see a live demo of saponification and how soap removes dirt, compare how different oils affect a bar, then melt, colour, scent and mould their own glycerin soap and test its pH. In Aroma Lab, participants learn the fragrance pyramid of top, middle and base notes, test 15 oils on smelling strips, then blend and bottle their own 10 ml roll-on perfume. Both workshops show how chemical engineering principles such as reactions, volatility and formulation apply to everyday products.
Approx time it takes for one student to: About 40 minutes for Saponify and 30 minutes for Aroma Lab.

Participation is individual: each participant makes one soap bar at Saponify or one 10 ml roll-on perfume at Aroma Lab, and may take part in both. Participants must register at the stall desk with a valid fest ID, collect a batch time, and report 5 minutes early. Latecomers may be shifted to a later batch, and walk-ins are allowed only if slots are open. Every session begins with a compulsory briefing and demonstration. Participants then move through the stations in order, following volunteer instructions and using only the fixed quantity of materials given to them. At Saponify, only volunteers operate the induction cooktop and handle the melted soap base, and participants pour under supervision. Every participant who completes the session receives a participation certificate, and the coordinators' decision is final on all matters.

Event Description mention clearly and el:
This proposed event is a structured, zero-contact 3v3 laser tag tournament designed for efficient participant turnover, clear operational boundaries, and strict safety compliance. Matches are played in strictly timed 5-to-10-minute rounds within a custom-built, temporary arena featuring fixed physical barriers and defensive cover points. The tournament utilizes a dynamic, multi-layered scoring system: teams earn base points for eliminating opponents and receive time-remaining bonus multipliers for quick squad eliminations, but face strict point deductions for every verified electronic hit they sustain. To further elevate the game's complexity, an interactive retrieval mechanic is integrated. Hidden objects are strategically scattered throughout the arena, allowing players to earn significant bonus points by successfully locating them while actively evading enemy fire. All match data is continuously tracked on a centralized leaderboard to determine overall tournament standings.

To ensure dynamic gameplay and complete operational control, strict arena rules are enforced by dedicated referees. All physical obstacles are strictly stationary; players cannot move, alter, or climb them, nor can they use them to physically block opponents. Gameplay mechanics require a clear line of sight for all valid hits, explicitly prohibiting blind firing around corners or shooting through structural gaps. Additionally, an anti-camping protocol mandates that players cannot remain behind a single obstacle for more than 30 seconds without moving, which naturally encourages continuous exploration for the hidden objects. Because the event relies entirely on non-projectile electronic blasters and wearable sensors, it carries zero physical or projectile risks, guaranteeing a highly controlled and safe environment for the venue.

Event Description mention clearly and el:
SDC Games is a two-day, multi-domain technical and non-technical competition organized by the Software Development Club (SDC) as part of Technozion 2026. The event is designed to test participants across different areas of technology while also incorporating elements of creativity, problem-solving, teamwork, strategy, and observation.

The event consists of four technical domains - AI/ML, Coding, Cyber Security, and Web Development, and two non-technical domains: Design and PR.

Day 1 – Multi-Domain Challenge

Day 1 consists of four rounds. Three rounds are technical and are conducted in parallel by the four technical wings, while the third round is a common fun and entertainment round conducted jointly by the Design and PR teams.

For each technical round, participants can choose any one of the four technical domains according to their interest and attempt the challenge conducted by that domain. However, a participant cannot choose the same technical domain more than once across the technical rounds of Day 1. This allows participants to explore different domains and compete in multiple areas.

The technical challenges are designed with increasing levels of difficulty, with each subsequent challenge within a domain being more advanced than its preceding level. The technical rounds include quizzes, debugging, reverse coding, web development challenges, cybersecurity challenges, OSINT-based tasks, AI/ML puzzles, and location-based problem-solving activities.

The third round is a non-technical fun round, jointly conducted by the Design and PR teams, and is intended to provide a break from the technical challenges while testing participants through an engaging and interactive activity.

Participants' performance across the Day 1 rounds will contribute to their cumulative score. Based on the overall cumulative performance, participants will be shortlisted for the Day 2 challenges.

Day 2 – Common Cross-Domain Challenge

Day 2 brings the shortlisted participants together for common challenges that combine multiple technical domains. Instead of competing within a single domain, participants will be required to apply knowledge from different areas such as AI/ML, Web Development, Coding, Cyber Security, logic, observation, and teamwork.

The proposed Day 2 challenges are designed as immersive, scenario-based competitions where participants must solve interconnected problems, make strategic decisions, collaborate with teammates, and apply concepts from multiple technical domains to progress through the challenge.

Overall, SDC Games aims to provide participants with a unique competitive experience where they are not restricted to a single technical domain. The event combines technical knowledge with creativity, logical thinking, problem-solving, teamwork, strategy, and real-world application, making it an engaging multi-domain competition for Technozion 2026.

Event Description mention clearly and el:
Ever wanted to be a hacker? Break into enemy systems, seize control, and claim what's not yours — all while keeping your own turf safe from everyone trying to do the same to you. DEFCON 2.0 is HAM ARC's live attack-and-defense hacking hackathon, a full-scale cyber battleground where teams go head-to-head over real machines, real vulnerabilities, and real consequences. This isn't a simulation or a slideshow — it's hands-on, live, and happening right in front of you.

Every team gets a machine to defend and a battlefield of rivals to hunt. The mission is simple: find their weaknesses before they find yours, break in first, and take control — all while making sure your own machine doesn't fall to the team gunning for you. It's a constant push and pull between offense and defense, and the team that plays it best walks away as the top hacking crew on campus.

DEFCON 2.0 is brought to you by HAM ARC, and it's built to be intense, competitive, and unforgettable. Whether you're the one breaking in or the one holding the line, this is where you find out what you're really capable of.

Step into the arena. Prove you've got what it takes to hack your way to the top.
Rules of the Event, include how many rou:
Rules of the Event

Format & Rounds

1. Round 1 — Fortify
   Teams receive their assigned machine and a fixed window of time to inspect it, close obvious vulnerabilities, and shore up their defenses. No attacking is allowed during this round — it's purely about securing your own system before the fight begins.

2. Round 2 — Attack
   The arena goes live. All team machines are now visible and attackable on the network. From this point on, it's attack-only — scan for weak or poorly-defended machines, break in, escalate access, and try to gain full control before your rivals do the same to you.

3. Round 3 — Reckoning (if applicable, based on final format)
   Final scoring and results based on how deep each team penetrated rival systems and how well they held their own. Top teams may face a tiebreaker or a live showcase round.

(Exact number of rounds and timing will be confirmed closer to the event based on final turnout and infrastructure — check event-day updates.)

Team Composition
- Teams of 1–4 members.
- Each team is given one attack workstation (private, not accessible to others) and one defended machine (the one rival teams will be attacking).

Core Rules
- Only attack machines belonging to opposing teams within the official arena network. Attacking organizers' infrastructure, the scoring system, or anything outside the designated network is strictly forbidden.
- No denial-of-service attacks — crashing or flooding a machine is not allowed. The objective is compromise, not disruption.
- Do not attack or interfere with another team's attack workstation — only their defended machine is a valid target.
- Compromise milestones (initial foothold, privilege escalation, full control) are automatically detected and scored by the system — there's no manual flag submission.
- Sharing exploits, credentials, or access with other teams is not permitted.
- Organizers reserve the right to disqualify any team found exploiting the arena's boundaries or the scoring system itself, rather than the actual challenge machines.

Scoring
- Points are awarded for successful intrusions, depth of compromise (foothold → escalation → full control), and speed.
- Points are also awarded for successfully defending your machine — detecting intrusions, blocking attacks, or staying uncompromised.
- Final standings are based on total points at the end of the Attack round.

Event Description mention clearly and el:
Business Frenzy is an interactive business strategy simulation combining product building, trading, market analysis and pitching.

In this edition, the central product will be a smartphone. Teams will build their product using feature cards, manage a limited budget, respond to changing market conditions, negotiate with other teams and finally pitch their product to a panel of judges.

At the beginning, each team will receive a fixed virtual purse and a random set of feature cards representing different smartphone specifications, such as:

Display: Standard / AMOLED / High Refresh Rate / Foldable
Camera: Single / Dual / Triple / Professional
Processor: Entry-level / Mid-range / Flagship / Next-gen
Audio: Standard / Stereo / Hi-Fi / Spatial Audio

Each feature will have different levels of quality and a corresponding reference price set by the organisers.

Teams will analyse their initial cards and select a target customer segment, such as budget, mass-market, premium or flagship consumers. They will then enter a trading phase, where they can buy, sell and exchange cards with other teams.

The reference price will act as a baseline, but teams can negotiate and trade at higher or lower prices depending on demand and scarcity.

Market Shocks

After the initial trading round, the organisers will introduce Market News that changes the attractiveness of certain technologies or customer segments.

For example, a breakthrough in fast-charging technology could suddenly increase the value of advanced battery technology.

Teams will then participate in an auction for newly introduced technology cards, forcing them to decide how much of their remaining budget they are willing to spend on the latest innovation.

Further trading rounds will allow teams to restructure their products according to the changing market conditions.

Multiple cycles of this will be there

 Final Pitch

After the final trading phase, teams will lock in their product and pitch it to the judges.

The pitch must cover:

* Product concept
* Target audience
* Features and specifications
* Pricing
* Product-market fit
* Response to changing market conditions
* Why customers should choose their product

The objective is not simply to build the most expensive or technologically advanced product, but to create a product whose features, price and target market form a strong and logical business strategy.
Rules of the Event, include how many rou:
General Rules

1. Participants will compete in teams.
2. Each team will receive a fixed virtual purse and a random set of feature cards.
3. Every card will have a feature category, specification and organiser-defined reference price.
4. Teams must use their cards and acquired resources to build one final product.
5. Teams are responsible for maintaining their cash and card records.
6. Virtual money has no value outside the event.

Event Structure

The event will broadly follow:

1. Initial Card Distribution
2. Target Market Selection
3. Initial Trading Round
4. Market News
5. New Technology Auction
6. Trading Round
7. Further Market News / Auctions / Trading
8. Product Lock-in
9. Final Pitch & Q&A

The number of Market News, Auction and Trading cycles is not fixed and will be determined by the organisers based on the event schedule and gameplay.

Initial Distribution & Target Market

1. Initial cards will be distributed randomly.
2. Teams cannot choose their initial cards.
3. Teams will receive a limited time to analyse their resources.
4. Each team must identify an initial target market.
5. Teams may change their target market later if changing market conditions make it strategically viable.

Trading Rules

1. Trading is permitted only during designated trading rounds.
2. Teams may trade with any other participating team.
3. Organisers will provide a reference price for every card.
4. Teams may negotiate prices above or below the reference price.
5. Competitive bidding between teams is allowed.
6. A transaction is valid only when both teams agree and it is recorded/verified by the organisers.
7. No trades may be conducted once the trading round has officially ended.

Market News

1. At predetermined points, organisers will release Market News.
2. News may increase or decrease the demand for specific technologies, introduce new technology, create scarcity or change consumer preferences.
3. Teams will receive a limited time to analyse each news event before the next phase begins.

Technology Auctions

1. New technology cards introduced through Market News will be auctioned by the organisers.
2. Each auction will have a starting price, bidding increment and time limit.
3. The highest valid bidder wins the card.
4. The amount spent will be deducted from the team's purse.
5. Teams must manage their remaining budget for subsequent trading rounds.

Card Limits & Discarding

1. A maximum number of cards may be held within each feature category, as specified by the organisers.
2. Teams exceeding this limit must sell or discard cards before acquiring additional cards in that category.
3. Unwanted cards may be sold back to the organisers during designated periods at their reference price.
4. A discarded technology may become valuable again after a later Market News event.

 Final Product & Pitch

Before the final pitch, teams must lock in:

* Final feature cards
* Target audience
* Product name
* Selling price
* Product positioning

No modifications will be allowed after the product is locked.

Each team will receive a fixed amount of time for its pitch, followed by a short Q&A with the judges.

Hidden messages are written in invisible ink and can be read only under UV torchlight, and latent fingerprint evidence is also present at the scene. Chromatography is run a day in advance and the developed results are placed in the crime room as physical evidence. Participants can play individually or in teams of up to 3. Each team first attends a briefing covering the story, evidence locations and the QR codes linked to the evidence. Then they get 15 minutes inside the crime scene room to observe and collect evidence, followed by 15 minutes in the writing room to write up what happened, how it happened, and why. Submissions are then evaluated and the winner is announced. There are no other rules beyond the time limit, since the focus is on observation, deduction and teamwork.

Event Description mention clearly and el:
The event is a collection of interactive AI/ML-based challenges designed to make participants explore and apply concepts from Computer Vision, Deep Learning, NLP, LLMs, RAG, Prompt Engineering, and AI Agent Orchestration through practical and competitive experiences.

1. Motion Rush : AI Powered Full-Body Gaming

Motion Rush is an interactive game inspired by Subway Surfers, where instead of using a keyboard or controller, participants control the game using their whole-body movements. The system will capture the participant’s body posture and movements using MediaPipe, process the extracted landmarks using Deep Learning models such as CNN + LSTM, and convert recognized movements into keyboard inputs using PyAutoGUI.

A major focus of the challenge is handling real-world computer vision problems such as different lighting conditions, camera positioning, body detection, movement differentiation, noisy predictions, and accurate real time tracking. If required, Transformer-based architectures can also be explored as an alternative to LSTM.

Participants will receive a score based on their game performance, accuracy, and completion/time based performance. A live leaderboard will display the rankings of participants based on their verified scores, creating a competitive environment throughout the event. The objective is to demonstrate how Deep Learning and Computer Vision can be converted into an engaging real-world interactive application.

2. Clash of Minds : AI-Based Argument Evaluation

Clash of Minds is a structured, AI assisted argumentation challenge in which two participants debate a given topic. The system follows a half-duplex interaction, where one participant presents an argument first, after which the system evaluates it before allowing the next response.

The AI evaluates multiple dimensions of the conversation, including factual correctness, relevance to the given topic, logical flow, whether the participant is responding to the opponent, and whether the discussion is deviating from the topic. A RAG based automated pipeline will verify factual claims against reliable browser-based sources. The system will also analyze whether both participants are actually listening to and building upon each other’s arguments rather than simply presenting unrelated points.

3. LLM Jailbreak : AI Security Challenge

LLM Jailbreak is a prompt engineering and AI-security challenge where participants attempt to make an AI system reveal information that it has been instructed to protect. The challenge focuses on understanding LLM behaviour, prompt injection, instruction hierarchy, context manipulation, and AI safety mechanisms.

Participants will interact with a protected AI system within a fixed time limit and attempt to achieve the required objective through creative interaction and prompt engineering. The system will evaluate the interaction and determine the extent to which the participant was able to bypass the model’s restrictions.

Participants will receive partial scores for successfully recovering individual protected pieces of information, with the final score determined by the predefined scoring system. A live leaderboard will rank participants based on their verified scores, with completion time used as a tie-breaker where required. This will allow participants to compete while also encouraging creative and efficient prompt engineering.

4. LLM Orchestration – Multi-Agent Prompt Engineering Challenge

This is a team-based challenge involving three participants and three specialized AI agents. Each participant is responsible for a different stage of a larger problem, and the output generated by one participant/agent becomes the input for the next.

Each agent will have a specific role and may have access to specialized tools such as OCR/Vision, NetworkX, or Z3/OR-Tools. The participants must design prompts that allow their respective agents to perform their assigned task while respecting the constraints imposed by the system.

The final output will be evaluated against an expected answer, allowing the team to receive an accuracy score. The team’s verified score will be displayed on a live team leaderboard, where teams will be ranked according to their final pipeline accuracy. In case of equal scores, completion time can be used as a tie-breaker.

This makes participants think not only about individual prompts but also about how information should be passed, transformed, and constrained across a complete AI pipeline.

5. Chromatic Action Matching – Deep Learning & Computer Vision

Chromatic Action Matching is an interactive Computer Vision and Deep Learning demonstration designed to introduce participants to important concepts such as CNNs, OpenCV, image processing, feature extraction, and visual recognition.

Participants will perform specific actions or movements in front of a camera, and the system will process the visual input to identify and match the corresponding action. A celebrity-themed example can also be incorporated to make the experience more engaging and relatable.

Participants will receive a score based on the number and accuracy of correctly recognized actions. Their verified scores will be displayed on a leaderboard, allowing participants to compare their performance and encouraging repeated attempts to improve their score.

Although this will not be the flagship competition of the event, it serves an important educational purpose by allowing participants to experience fundamental Computer Vision and Deep Learning concepts through an interactive application rather than only through theoretical demonstrations.

Overall Event Leaderboard

In addition to the individual leaderboard for each challenge, the event will maintain a common overall leaderboard. Scores from the different challenges will be normalized to a common scale because the games have different scoring mechanisms.

Participants who complete multiple eligible challenges can accumulate their normalized scores on the overall leaderboard. This creates a broader competition across the entire event while still allowing each individual challenge to maintain its own ranking.

The overall event therefore aims to create a hands on, competitive and educational AI environment where participants do not simply observe AI technologies but actively interact with them, design solutions, experiment with models, and understand how modern AI systems handle real-world challenges.

Prizes in form of goodies will be given to winner of each competetive model(except clash of minds) and top 3 accumulated score winners.

Event Description mention clearly and el:
"EcoCity: Build to Last" is a sustainability-simulation game, where teams use a fixed budget to build a resilient city. The ultimate goal is long-term survival, not maximizing the budget spent; a lean, well-balanced city will outperform an overbuilt, resource-hungry one.
Game Mechanics
 * City Building: During a 45-minute build phase, teams purchase land, housing, agriculture, water facilities, and employment infrastructure via a built-in catalogue.
 * The Energy Trade-Off: Participants must balance cheap, highly polluting, and depletable coal against expensive, clean, and renewable wind or solar power.
 * Population: Population growth is automatic but strictly capped by the city's tightest resource whether that is housing, food, water, or jobs.
Simulation and Judging
 * The Engine: A deterministic, rule-based engine simulates the city year-by-year, tracking resource balances, coal reserves, and a pollution index.
 * Winning: The simulation stops if the city hits a resource deficit for consecutive years, crosses a pollution threshold, or if the population drops to zero. The longest-surviving city wins, capped at a 300-year "Sustainable" horizon.
 * Tie-Breakers: Ties are settled by the lowest peak pollution, followed by the lowest total spend.
Event Logistics
The 90-minute event relies on a lightweight, browser-based web app, allowing participants to use a Bring-Your-Own-Device (BYOD) format. It concludes with a live, on-screen simulation reveal, optionally featuring an AI-generated narrative explaining the rise and fall of each city.

 * Population Limits: Population grows automatically but is capped by the city's tightest resource—whether that is housing, food, water, or jobs.

Event Description mention clearly and el:
Mechatronics Gala

Mechatronics Gala is a flagship multi-event showcase organized under Technozion, NIT Warangal's technical festival, bringing together autonomous racing, aerial piloting, and human-vs-AI gameplay under one banner. Designed as three tiered experiences, the Gala caters to participants at every stage of the robotics journey — from experienced builders bringing their own hardware, to intermediate enthusiasts getting hands-on flight experience, to complete beginners exploring AI decision-making for the first time. Across all three events, the Gala emphasizes hands-on learning in robotics, perception, planning, and control, while providing a fair, safe, and exciting platform that builds a community around autonomous systems and showcases these technologies to the wider festival audience.

Turing Track — For the Experienced

Turing Track, hosted by the HAM ARC Club, is an autonomous car racing competition inspired by the F1TENTH/RoboRacer format. Teams — including those from outside colleges — bring their own small-scale autonomous vehicles (max 60×40×30 cm, 5 kg) and race them on a closed circuit with no human intervention or remote control during the timed run, competing for cash prizes. For students within the host college who don't have their own hardware, the event also provides an in-house AGV rig so they can test and tune their autonomous software on real equipment. The competition runs in two stages: a qualifying time trial (3 solo timed attempts, fastest lap counts, top 8 or top 25% advance) followed by head-to-head elimination finals (quarterfinals → semifinals → final, 2 cars racing simultaneously per heat). Vehicles may use LiDAR, cameras, IMUs, and wheel encoders, running any onboard compute (Jetson, Pi, NUC, custom) with software stacks like ROS, Pure Pursuit, MPC, RL, or Imitation Learning — as long as all processing stays fully onboard. Safety is enforced via mandatory E-Stops, fire-safe battery handling, and a structured penalty system, with prizes for the top three finishers plus special recognitions for Fastest Qualifying Lap and Best Design/Most Innovative Approach.



AI Gambit — For the Curious Beginner

AI Gambit is the Gala's most accessible tier, an interactive showcase where a human participant faces off head-to-head, solo, against a custom-built 6-DOF robotic arm (LeRobot SO-101) in a game of their choice — Chess, Connect Four, or cube-stacking. An overhead camera and OpenCV-based vision system track the board in real time; once the participant makes their move and signals turn completion, the system calculates the robot's optimal counter-move using Imitation Learning policies combined with inverse kinematics and path planning, then the arm physically grasps and moves the piece before retracting for the next turn — with the AI's decision-making displayed live, giving participants a transparent window into how the machine "thinks." Scoring is by match result (win > draw > loss) and speed for strategy games, or accuracy and completion time for precision challenges, with tied winners settled via a sudden-death speed round. Safety is built around an enclosed workspace, a continuously-monitored hardware/software E-Stop, and torque-limited servos to prevent pinch hazards. Open to all registered Technozion attendees with walk-in registration available, the event awards a "Grandmaster" title plus prizes to the top three, alongside a live leaderboard at the booth.


Mach Sprint — For the Intermediate

Mach Sprint (the Litewing Drone Challenge) adapts Turing Track's two-stage racing framework to aerial piloting, testing manual dexterity, spatial awareness, and speed rather than autonomy. Teams — including those from outside colleges — can bring their own drones to race on the indoor obstacle course. Since transporting drones is often impractical, the Gala also provides its own event-standard ESP-32 Litewing drones, so participants without hardware can still get genuine hands-on piloting experience, controlling the drone entirely via a smartphone app over its local Wi-Fi (no RC transmitters or FPV goggles allowed). The course spans a 30–80 m closed loop with a minimum 3 m × 3 m flight clearance, featuring gates, over-under hurdles, sweeping turns, and at least one tight chicane. The format mirrors Turing Track: a qualifying time trial (3 solo timed runs, top 8 or top 25% advance) followed by head-to-head elimination finals (quarterfinals → semifinals → final, 2 drones racing simultaneously per heat). Teams get a dedicated practice window to familiarize themselves with the controls before their timed runs. Safety centers on a mandatory smartphone kill-switch, fire-safe battery handling, and a graduated penalty system (+5s for skipped gates, +10s for collisions, +15s for marshal repositioning, DNF after 3+ incidents), with prizes TBA for the top three teams.

Build a car powered entirely by chemistry — no batteries, no motors, and no mechanical brakes. Teams design a small vehicle (within 40×30×20 cm) propelled by a chemical reaction of their choice, and engineer a second reaction to stop it precisely, with no timers, or manual control involved once it's released. 
The twist: your target distance and payload are revealed just an hour before your run, so your chemistry has to be tunable on the spot, not fixed in advance. Scoring rewards precision, not speed — closest stop to the line wins.

Thermal Armor is a competitive thermal-protection-system design challenge in which teams act as materials 
and engineering teams developing a lightweight, low-cost thermal shield for a small re-entry capsule. Teams 
design, build, test, analyze, redesign and retest their prototype, with performance measured using a 
standardized testing setup.
Rules of the Event, include how many rou:
1)Design — 10 minutes to select materials, plan the layer configuration and allocate the virtual budget.
2)Build — 20 minutes to physically construct the thermal protection system.
3)Test — each team is tested using the same heat source, payload, distance, starting temperature and 
exposure time.
4)Failure Analysis — teams review their temperature results and identify why their design performed as it 
did.
5)Redesign & Retest — teams make limited improvements and test again under the same conditions.

Event Description mention clearly and el:
ARCADE is an interactive robotics and embedded-systems challenge organized by the Robotics Club. The event combines algorithm development, simulation, embedded implementation, and real-time robotic systems through two challenges: AI Air Hockey and Robot Strike.

Participants will not simply operate pre-built systems. They will be given the problem statement and the required system behavior, and will be expected to develop the key algorithm or control logic required to solve the challenge. Depending on the event setup and time available, participants may first validate their approach through MATLAB-based simulation and subsequently implement or test the algorithm on real-time embedded hardware/circuits.

The event is designed to provide participants with practical exposure to the process of converting a problem statement into an algorithm, validating it through simulation, and deploying it on a physical robotic system.
Rules of the Event, include how many rou:
General Rules
ARCADE consists of two independent challenges: AI Air Hockey and Robot Strike.
Participants will be provided with a problem statement, system specifications, constraints, and the required interfaces.
Participants are expected to develop the essential algorithm/control logic required to solve the assigned challenge.
The organizers may provide the basic hardware interface, simulation framework, or supporting code. Participants will be required to implement only the designated portions of the solution.
Participants may be given the opportunity to simulate and validate their algorithms in MATLAB or the designated simulation environment before testing them on the physical system.
Based on the event setup and available time, successful solutions may be tested on the real-time embedded/robotic hardware.
Evaluation may consider factors such as accuracy, response time, stability, successful task completion, and overall algorithm performance.
Participants must work within the given time limit and system constraints.
Use of pre-written or externally sourced solutions may be restricted and will be specified by the organizers before the event.
Participants must not modify the hardware or supporting system unless explicitly permitted.
In case of a technical issue with the provided hardware or infrastructure, the organizers may reset the system or provide an additional attempt.
The decision of the event coordinators regarding rule violations, technical issues, and evaluation will be final.
AI Air Hockey
Participants will develop the required algorithm for an autonomous robotic air-hockey player.
The problem may involve tasks such as puck tracking, position estimation, prediction, decision-making, or robotic paddle control.
The solution will first be evaluated in simulation, where applicable.
A successful algorithm may then be deployed on the real-time system consisting of the Raspberry Pi, ESP-based controller, sensors/camera, and robotic mechanism.
The final performance will be evaluated based on the ability of the robotic system to respond correctly to the puck and perform the assigned task.
The exact scoring criteria, time limit, and number of attempts will be announced before the event.
Robot Strike
Robot Strike consists of three progressive rounds, with increasing levels of control and targeting difficulty.

Round 1 – Stationary Target

The participant develops the required control/aiming algorithm for hitting a stationary target.
The solution may be validated through simulation before being tested on the robotic arm.

Round 2 – Linear Moving Target

The target moves along a predefined linear path.
Participants must modify or develop the required algorithm to account for the target's position and movement.
The solution will be evaluated through simulation and/or real-time hardware testing, depending on the event setup.

Round 3 – Dynamic Moving Target

The target follows a circular or dynamically varying movement pattern.
Participants must develop an appropriate tracking, prediction, or control strategy to successfully hit the target.
This round represents the highest level of difficulty.
Procedure
Participants receive the challenge statement and technical specifications.
The required algorithmic problem and available interfaces are explained.
Participants develop the required code/control algorithm.
The solution is tested through MATLAB simulation or the designated simulation environment, where applicable.
Participants may refine their solution based on the simulation results.
The final solution is tested on the real-time robotic/embedded system, where applicable.
Performance is evaluated according to the predefined scoring criteria.
Participants must follow all safety instructions while interacting with the physical robotic systems.

​The Gameplay & Challenge
​Participants sit before the "Neural Core"—a sealed chamber containing ferrofluid, mounted above a high-power electromagnetic array.
​The Goal: The player must sustain intense cognitive focus for 10 consecutive seconds.
​The Interaction: As the player's concentration increases, their brainwaves trigger a proportional increase in the magnetic flux density. The dead pool of ferrofluid instantly erupts into organic, geometric spikes, growing taller and sharper as focus intensifies.
​The Challenge: Holding a consistent mental state is difficult. If the player's focus wavers or breaks, the magnetic field collapses, and the spikes instantly dissolve.
​The Spectacle: An adjacent monitor displays the participant's real-time brainwave frequencies and a live focus meter, allowing the crowd to see the direct correlation between the participant's mental state and the physical matter morphing on the table.

Bid to Build is an engaging civil engineering challenge testing strategic resource allocation, design estimation, and architectural execution under real-world project constraints.

Participants analyze engineering requirements, bid on material and construction resources, and build structural prototypes evaluated on stability, efficiency, and cost effectiveness.
Rules of the Event, include how many rou:
1. Teams will consist of 2 to 4 participants.
2. In Round 1, teams participate in a bidding session to allocate materials and construction resources within a specified virtual budget.
3. In Round 2, teams construct their model using only acquired resources within the allocated time.
4. Prototypes will be load-tested and judged on strength-to-weight ratio, structural integrity, and budget adherence.
5. General fest guidelines and safety protocols must be followed at all times.
